pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — How Fossils Form (ages 7–9): explain the basic sequence of fossilisation — an organism dies and is QUICKLY BURIED in sediment; over a very long time minerals seep in and replace the remains while the sediment hardens to rock, preserving the shape — and understand that fossilisation is RARE.
• Standards — UK (DfE): direct anchor — Y3 'Rocks' (recognise that fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock); uses correct vocabulary (sediment, minerals, rock).
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports grade-3 3-LS4-1 (fossils as evidence of past life) and the MS-ESS/MS-LS fossil-record strand; the process explains why the fossil record is patchy.
• Operational details — Teach as an ordered CAUSAL sequence with conditions, not just a list: (1) death; (2) RAPID burial in sediment (mud/sand) — the critical step, because exposed remains rot or are scavenged; (3) soft parts decay, hard parts (bone/shell/teeth) remain; (4) over millions of years, groundwater minerals permeate/replace the remains (permineralisation) and sediment compacts into rock; (5) uplift and erosion later expose it. Emphasise WHY it's rare (most organisms never get buried fast enough) so children understand the fossil record is incomplete — a key later idea. Keep timescales as 'millions of years' with relative framing.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7): orders the basic steps (dies → buried → turns to rock over a long time). Tier B (~8): explains why quick burial matters (otherwise it rots/is eaten) and uses sediment/minerals/rock correctly. Tier C (~9): explains that minerals replace the remains over millions of years and that fossilisation is rare, so most living things leave no fossil.
bestPractices: Teach it as a conditional CAUSAL chain (each step enables the next), foregrounding rapid burial as the make-or-break step.
Make rarity explicit — have children reason that most animals rot or are eaten, so only a tiny fraction fossilise; this seeds 'the fossil record is incomplete'.
Distinguish soft parts (usually lost) from hard parts (bone, teeth, shell) that typically fossilise, explaining why we mostly find skeletons.
Insist on correct vocabulary (sediment, minerals, rock, buried) used in context, per Y3 'Rocks'.
Use a compare-conditions approach (buried fast vs left exposed) so the necessity of burial is discovered, not asserted.
keyRepresentations: A staged cross-section: dead animal on a riverbed → layers of sediment pile on → minerals replace bone → rock with fossil → erosion exposes it.
A timeline slider showing 'millions of years' compressing the mineralisation step.
A 'fossil or lost?' branching diagram: buried quickly → fossil; left exposed → rots/scavenged → no fossil.
commonMisconceptions: 'Fossils are the original bone, unchanged' — minerals usually replace the remains; a fossil is rock in the shape of the original.
'Any dead animal becomes a fossil' — fossilisation is rare; most decay or are eaten before burial.
'Fossils form quickly' — mineral replacement and rock formation take (typically) millions of years.
'Soft parts fossilise as easily as bones' — usually only hard parts (bone, teeth, shell) survive; soft tissue rarely preserves.
'Fossils form on the surface where the animal died' — burial in sediment (often water-laid) is essential; surface remains are lost.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach fossilisation as an ordered CAUSAL chain with conditions: (1) an organism dies; (2) it is RAPIDLY BURIED in sediment (mud/sand) — the make-or-break step, because exposed remains rot or are scavenged; (3) soft parts decay while hard parts (bone, teeth, shell) remain; (4) over millions of years minerals carried by groundwater seep into the hard remains, filling tiny spaces and often gradually replacing the original material, while the sediment compacts and hardens into rock, preserving the shape; (5) later uplift and erosion expose it. Burial is necessary but does not guarantee a fossil. Make RARITY explicit so children reason that most living things leave no fossil, seeding the big idea that the fossil record is an incomplete, lucky sample. Use correct vocabulary (sediment, minerals, rock, buried) in context. The strongest proposed activity is intended to let children choose settings, with quick burial decided by setting-dependent chance, and run time forward so that rarity may become an observed outcome rather than a stated fact; staged diagrams and ordering/check tasks support the sequence and vocabulary.

activities.title: Play fate for a dead animal: vary conditions and run time forward
feedback: If a learner's quickly buried animal becomes a fossil, confirm: quick burial protected the hard parts from rotting and scavengers long enough for minerals to soak in and gradually replace them, and for the sediment to harden into rock. If a buried animal still leaves no fossil, explain that burial is needed but does not guarantee a fossil.
If a learner leaves the body exposed and gets 'no fossil', confirm: in the open it rotted or was eaten before it could be buried, so nothing was preserved.

When the tally shows only a few fossils from 20 animals, prompt: 'Why did so few become fossils?' Expected reasoning: most were never buried quickly enough, and even some buried ones did not last. If a tally is higher, compare settings and discuss that most animals die where quick burial is unlikely.

If a learner expects the bone to stay unchanged, point out the colour-shift step: minerals gradually fill and often replace the remains, so the fossil is usually mostly rock in the shape of the original bone, not the unchanged original bone.
activities.rationale: The key lesson — why fossilisation so rarely succeeds — is intended to be made concrete by running the process and comparing conditions (buried fast vs left exposed). Burial is decided by setting-dependent chance rather than chosen directly, so the necessity of burial may be reasoned out rather than asserted, and rarity may appear as an observed outcome. This is a proposed format, not a separately validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Fossilisation typically requires rapid burial in sediment before decay/scavenging; over long periods minerals permeate and replace hard remains (permineralisation) as sediment lithifies to rock; soft tissues rarely preserve, so fossilisation is rare and the record is incomplete.
learnerActions: For each of about 20 animals, choose where the body falls (e.g. muddy river delta, dry plain, open ground); the model then decides by chance whether sediment covers it quickly or it is left exposed. The odds depend on the setting: quick burial is more likely in a muddy delta and unlikely on dry open ground.
Advance a time dial forward through 'millions of years' and watch what happens for each choice.

For buried-quickly cases, observe the sequence: soft parts fade, hard parts (bone/teeth/shell) remain, minerals seep in and the bone colour-shifts to 'stone', sediment layers compact and harden into rock, then uplift and erosion reveal the fossil. Notice that some buried cases still end with no fossil (for example, the bone dissolves or the rock is later worn away), and some fossils are never exposed.
For left-exposed cases, observe scavengers and decay strip the body to nothing — 'no fossil'.
Keep a running tally of how many of the 20 animals became fossils, then state in your own words why fossils are rare.
Label each stage with the correct words: sediment, minerals, rock, buried.
activities.intendedInsight: Fossilisation is a conditional sequence in which rapid burial before decay is the crux. Burial is needed but not a guarantee, and because most animals are never buried fast enough, only a tiny lucky fraction fossilise, so the fossil record is incomplete.

activities.title: Compare buried vs exposed: the 'fossil or lost?' branch
feedback: If the learner predicts both become fossils, contrast the two paths: only the buried one is protected from rotting and scavengers.
Reinforce that 'exposed' usually ends in 'no fossil', which is why most animals leave none.
activities.rationale: A direct compare-conditions task is intended to foreground rapid burial as the make-or-break step and may let the necessity of burial be discovered through contrast rather than assertion.
sourceClaims: Fossilisation typically requires rapid burial in sediment before decay/scavenging; over long periods minerals permeate and replace hard remains (permineralisation) as sediment lithifies to rock; soft tissues rarely preserve, so fossilisation is rare and the record is incomplete.
learnerActions: Look at two identical animals that die in the same place; one is buried quickly by sediment, the other is left on the surface.
Predict what will happen to each after a very long time, and say why.
Trace a branching diagram: buried quickly → hard parts remain → minerals replace them → rock → fossil; left exposed → rots/scavenged → no fossil.
Explain in one sentence why quick burial is the step that makes the difference.
activities.intendedInsight: Burial before decay is the pivotal condition that determines whether anything is preserved at all.

activities.title: Read the staged cross-section and label soft vs hard parts
feedback: If a learner labels soft parts as fossilising, explain that soft tissue usually decays, so bone, teeth and shell are what normally remain.
Check that each stage is retold in the correct order and that the vocabulary is used in context.
activities.rationale: A labelled staged diagram is intended to teach the ordered sequence and the soft-vs-hard distinction cleanly; note it shows one fixed successful path, so it cannot by itself let a learner test failure conditions — pair it with a conditions-varying task that may help make rarity observable.
sourceClaims: Fossilisation typically requires rapid burial in sediment before decay/scavenging; over long periods minerals permeate and replace hard remains (permineralisation) as sediment lithifies to rock; soft tissues rarely preserve, so fossilisation is rare and the record is incomplete.
learnerActions: Study a staged cross-section: dead animal on a riverbed → layers of sediment pile on → minerals replace the bone → rock holding a fossil → erosion exposes it.
Reveal each stage's caption in order and retell the sequence aloud using the words sediment, minerals, and rock.
On a picture of an organism, label which parts are soft (usually lost) and which are hard — bone, teeth, shell — and typically survive.
Explain why we mostly find skeletons rather than whole animals.
activities.intendedInsight: The ordered sequence of fossilisation, and why hard parts are usually what we find because soft tissue rarely preserves.

activities.title: Order the stages and explain why burial matters (check)
feedback: Full response: explains the sequence AND that rapid burial before decay is the crux, that minerals replace the remains over millions of years, and that this is why fossils are rare — transferring to the garden-bone or open-ground counterexample.
Partial response: lists steps (dies, buried, turns to rock) but cannot explain why quick burial matters or why fossils are rare — recites a sequence without the mechanism; prompt for the 'why'.

Gap/misconception — 'any dead animal becomes a fossil, bones just slowly turn into fossils': contrast the millions of animals that have died with the few fossils found, and make burial-before-decay the pivotal step using the rotting-in-the-open image.

Misconception — 'the real bones are still there, just very old and hard': introduce mineral replacement — over millions of years, minerals from groundwater soak in and the original material is often gradually swapped for rock minerals, so the fossil is usually stone in the shape of the bone rather than the unchanged bone.
Misconception — timescale collapse ('fossils form in a few years'): anchor the millions-of-years timescale with the sediment-turning-to-rock step; a buried bone next year is still just a buried bone.

Follow-up probes: 'Why don't we find fossils of most animals that ever lived?'; 'If you buried a chicken bone in your garden, would it be a fossil next year? Why not?' (treat as a relative, condition-dependent teaching device, not an absolute); 'What does the word sediment actually mean?'; 'Where do the minerals come from?'
activities.rationale: An ordering plus short-answer check is intended to confirm the process and may surface specific misconceptions; it verifies rather than builds the process intuition, so use it after the hands-on and diagram tasks.
learnerActions: Put the stages in the correct order: dies → buried in sediment → minerals replace the remains → sediment hardens to rock → erosion exposes it.
Answer: why don't most animals that die become fossils?
Answer: what happens to the original hard parts over millions of years?

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: 'A dinosaur dies out in the open on dry ground and its body just lies there. Millions of years pass. Will there be a fossil of it? Say yes or no — and explain what has to happen for a fossil to form.'
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate and check the sequence, the role of rapid burial, mineral replacement, and the rarity of fossils.

constraints: Keep timescales as 'millions of years' with relative framing appropriate to ages 7–9; a buried bone 'next year' is not a fossil.
Teach as an ordered causal chain where each step enables the next, foregrounding rapid burial as the make-or-break step; do not present fossilisation as a mere list.
Make rarity explicit and have children reason it out (most animals rot or are eaten before burial) rather than simply being told.
Distinguish soft parts (usually lost) from hard parts (bone, teeth, shell) that typically preserve; explain why we mostly find skeletons.
Insist on correct vocabulary — sediment, minerals, rock, buried — used in context, consistent with Y3 'Rocks'.
Clarify that a fossil is usually rock in the shape of the original remains after mineral replacement, not the unchanged original bone.

The staged cross-section is a scaffold that shows one fixed successful path; it cannot by itself let a learner test failure conditions, so it does not on its own convey rarity — pair it with a conditions-varying task.
An ordering/short-answer check confirms and assesses understanding; a learner can sequence correctly without grasping the mechanism, so probe the 'why' of burial and rarity.

The optional elements described (setting choice, time dial, colour-shift to stone, fossil tally, tap-to-reveal captions, buried/exposed flap) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms or specific products.
Water-laid sediment is common and useful as an example, but do not overstate conditions beyond 'burial in sediment before decay' as the general requirement.
State efficacy of any proposed activity format with proposed/may/intended wording; the formats here are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the single source is marked verified:false and was not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row ranked a 2D interactive 'ideal' and rated a 3D dig as adding 'cost without deepening' and dialogue as 'poor'. These are catalog fit preferences, not evidence of comparative efficacy or necessity; they are reframed here as scaffolds with stated limits and should not be read as universal pedagogical laws. A diagram or ordering/check task may teach or check the sequence and vocabulary but does not by itself let a learner vary the burial conditions and observe rarity as an outcome.

The garden-bone counterexample in the assessment assumes ordinary garden soil/short timescale; it is a reasonable teaching device for 'not a fossil next year', but exact burial outcomes depend on conditions — keep it as a relative, not absolute, claim.
One source citation underlies several activities; a citation supporting the general principle does not establish that any specific activity format was tested or is superior to another medium.
'Permineralisation' is used loosely in the source to mean minerals permeating and replacing remains; the age-appropriate simplification is retained, but strictly the two processes differ.

probeDeeper: Why don't we find fossils of most of the animals that have ever lived?
If you buried a chicken bone in your garden, would it be a fossil next year? Why not?
In your explanation, what does the word 'sediment' actually mean?
Where do the minerals come from that end up making the fossil?
assess.correctAnswer: Probably not. To become a fossil the body must be buried quickly in sediment before it rots or is eaten; then over millions of years minerals seep in and replace the remains while the sediment hardens into rock, keeping the shape. Left in the open it would decompose, so fossilisation is rare — most animals leave no fossil at all.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fossilisation is automatic and common: 'when animals die their bones just slowly turn into fossils over time.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the millions of animals that have died with the few fossils found; make burial-before-decay the pivotal step, using a rotting-in-the-open counter-image.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — when animals die their bones slowly turn into fossils.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'yes' with no mention of burial, sediment, or the rarity of fossils.

errorPatterns.pattern: A fossil is the actual original bone that simply got old and hard — no mineral replacement.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce mineral replacement: the original material is gradually swapped for rock minerals so the fossil is stone in the shape of the bone.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the real bones are still there, just very old and hard.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'yes, the real bones are still there, just very old,' with no idea that minerals replace the remains.

errorPatterns.pattern: Timescale collapse: fossils form in a few years.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the millions-of-years timescale with the sediment-turning-to-rock step; a buried bone next year is still just a buried bone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts fossilisation but says it happens quickly, e.g. within a lifetime or a few years.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks any dead animal becomes a fossil; makes no mention of burial or the vast timescale, and treats fossils as the leftover original bones.
responseLevels.full: Explains the sequence AND that rapid burial before decay is the crux, that minerals replace the remains over millions of years, and that this is why fossils are rare — transferring the reasoning to the garden-bone counterexample.
responseLevels.partial: Lists steps — dies, gets buried, turns to rock — but cannot explain why quick burial matters or why fossilisation is rare; recites a sequence without the mechanism.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A dinosaur dies out in the open on dry ground and its body just lies there. Millions of years pass. Will there be a fossil of it? Say yes or no — and explain what has to happen for a fossil to form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks any dead animal automatically becomes a fossil answers 'yes, the bones will slowly turn into a fossil' and never mentions burial. A child who understands the process names quick burial-before-decay as the crux and recognises that lying exposed means no fossil.
